reading.rtitle: Supplier Price Comparison -- Vetra Distribuzione, Finance Team
paras: Purpose. Two suppliers are on our shortlist for invoice approval software: Invent Match, from Brazil, and Clearbook, from the Netherlands. This note compares their public pricing pages for a team of 40 users.

Structure. Invent sells three tiers: Start, Growth and Enterprise. Clearbook, on the other hand, has one plan with optional add-ons. Invent's Growth tier includes the SAP connector, whereas Clearbook sells it as an add-on at 400 euros a month.

Price model. Invent charges per seat: 25 euros per user per month, billed annually, so 1,000 euros a month for us. Clearbook's price is usage-based: 0.08 euros for each invoice. With our current 6,000 invoices a month and the connector, Clearbook costs 880 euros a month and looks cheaper. However, our volume is expected to double by 2028, and Clearbook would then cost 1,360 euros a month.

One-time costs. Clearbook offers a 30-day free trial and no setup fee. Invent, however, charges a setup fee of 5,000 euros, which covers configuration and training. Unlike Clearbook, Invent does not offer a free trial. It offers a paid pilot of six weeks with our real invoices.

Risks. Clearbook's page does not mention support hours, while Invent's page includes support in English, Italian and Portuguese. We should ask Clearbook about hidden costs, such as storage or a second company in the group. Recommendation: ask both suppliers for a flat fee for the first year, so the offers can be compared on the same basis.

items.situation: Compare the two price models in one sentence: Invent / per seat / Clearbook / per invoice / whereas.
tips: Invent charges per seat, whereas Clearbook charges per invoice.
whereas joins two clauses, with a comma before it.

items.situation: Giulia says Clearbook is cheaper. Agree about today, then add the problem with however.
tips: You are right about today. However, their price grows with your volume.
However starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

items.situation: Say what Invent includes and Clearbook does not: unlike / the connector.
tips: Unlike Clearbook, we include the connector in the Growth tier.
unlike + a name or a noun.

items.situation: Start with while: their trial is free / our pilot uses real invoices.
tips: While their trial is free, our pilot uses your real invoices.

items.situation: The CFO asks about extra costs. Say there is no hidden cost for storage.
tips: Storage is included, so there is no hidden cost.

items.situation: Ask Giulia to compare both offers fairly.
tips: Can we compare both offers on the same basis?
on the same basis = with the same users, volume and years.

listenings.text: When I compare two software suppliers, I never start with the price on the page. Pricing pages are written to make every product look cheap. One supplier charges per seat, whereas the other charges per transaction, so the two numbers mean nothing side by side. The first thing I do is build one scenario: our number of users, our volume, and three years, not one. Then I look for the hidden costs. Is the connector included, or is it an add-on? Is there a setup fee? Is storage free? And finally, I ask both suppliers for a flat fee for the first year. The supplier that answers clearly, without changing the subject, usually wins. The cheapest page almost never does.

Last year a customer sent me a competitor's pricing page with one line: they are thirty percent cheaper. My first reaction was to offer a discount. I didn't. Instead, I asked for one hour to build a comparison on the same basis. Their price was usage-based, while ours was per seat. With the customer's real volume, they were cheaper in the first year. However, by the third year they were twenty percent more expensive. I sent a one-page table, with one difference per line and one sentence under each line. No adjectives, just numbers. The customer called me the next day and said: thank you, nobody explained it like that. We signed at our price. The discount was never discussed again.
